title: The Communitarian Critique

cards.h: The self is not an island
cards.b:
In the 1980s, a group of thinkers challenged Rawls and liberalism as a whole. They became known as communitarians.

The four big names are Michael Sandel, Alasdair MacIntyre, Charles Taylor and Michael Walzer. Interestingly, none of them liked the label much.

Their shared claim: liberalism starts from an abstract individual who chooses their own values. But real people are formed by their communities: family, religion, language, nation. A theory of justice must start there.

UPSC asks about this debate often, usually as "liberal vs communitarian" or as a critique of Rawls. It also connects to multiculturalism and group rights in India.

For liberals, the right is prior to the good. The state sets fair rules but stays neutral about what a good life is. Each person chooses for themselves.

Communitarians reply that we do not choose our deepest values from nowhere. We discover them in the communities that made us. A neutral state is impossible, and trying to be neutral weakens shared life.

Sandel, a Harvard professor, wrote Liberalism and the Limits of Justice (1982).

He says the people in Rawls's original position are unencumbered selves: selves with no attachments, standing apart from all their aims and loyalties.

But real people are encumbered. Some of our ties are not chosen but constitutive: they make us who we are. Being someone's child, or a member of a nation or faith, is not like picking a hobby.

Sandel also points to a problem in the difference principle. Rawls treats natural talents as a common asset. But that only makes sense if we already share a strong community. So Rawls quietly assumes the very community his theory leaves out.

Later, in Democracy's Discontent (1996) and The Tyranny of Merit (2020), Sandel argued for civic republicanism and against the arrogance of meritocracy.

MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) opens with a striking image. Imagine a world where science has been destroyed, and people use scientific words without understanding them. That, he says, is how we use moral words today.

Modern moral debate is interminable: people shout past each other because they have lost the shared framework that gave moral words meaning.

His answer is to return to Aristotle and the idea of virtues. Virtues make sense only inside:

  • Practices, like medicine, farming or chess, with their own standards of excellence.
  • The narrative unity of a human life.
  • A living tradition of argument passed between generations.

He ends darkly: we await "another, doubtless very different, St Benedict" to build communities that keep virtue alive.

Taylor is a Canadian philosopher.

"Atomism" (1979)

Liberals give individuals rights while denying they owe anything to society. But our very ability to be free, to choose and reason, can only develop in a society. So we have a duty to sustain it.

Sources of the Self (1989)

Identity is formed against a background of what matters, a "horizon" of meaning shared with others.

"The Politics of Recognition" (1992)

Identity is shaped by recognition, or its absence. Misrecognition can inflict real harm: it can imprison people in a false, demeaning picture of themselves. So minority cultures may deserve public recognition, as with French-speaking Quebec.

Walzer's Spheres of Justice (1983) rejects one single principle of justice for all goods.

Different goods have different social meanings, and so different rules of distribution:

  • Healthcare by need.
  • Office by merit.
  • Political power by persuasion and votes.
  • Commodities by the market.
  • Love by free affection.

Injustice is when one good dominates others. For example, money buying votes, court rulings or medical care. Walzer calls the goal complex equality: no single good converts into all others.

He adds that justice is relative to social meanings. It is found in a community's shared understandings, not deduced from an original position.

• Will Kymlicka, in Liberalism, Community and Culture (1989) and Multicultural Citizenship (1995), argued that liberalism can value culture. Culture gives us a context of choice. So minority rights can be defended on liberal grounds.
  • Rawls himself, in Political Liberalism (1993), said his theory was political, not a claim about human nature. The veil is a device of representation, not a description of real people.
  • Amy Gutmann warned that communitarians want us to live in Salem, but not to believe in witches: they like community but ignore how it can oppress.
  • Many now see a middle ground: liberal rights together with strong civic community.

• Conservatism: appeals to tradition can defend old hierarchies, such as caste, patriarchy or religious authority.
  • Which community? People belong to many communities that conflict. Who speaks for the community?
  • Oppression within groups: feminists like Susan Moller Okin, in "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?" (1997/1999), warned that group rights can trap women under patriarchal leaders.
  • Relativism: if justice is only shared meanings, how do we criticise an unjust society from within? Walzer replies that social critics work from the community's own ideals.

A balanced answer shows that both sides have learned from each other.

A separate strand, led by Amitai Etzioni, turned communitarian ideas into a political programme in the 1990s.

His The Spirit of Community (1993) and the Responsive Communitarian platform argued that rights must be balanced with responsibilities. Families, schools and neighbourhoods should rebuild moral voices.

This influenced the "Third Way" of Bill Clinton and Tony Blair, who spoke of "no rights without responsibilities".

In Asia, leaders like Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew invoked "Asian values": community, family and order over individual rights. Critics, including Amartya Sen, argued that Asian traditions also contain strong ideas of freedom and tolerance.

India's Constitution blends liberal and communitarian ideas.

  • Articles 25–28 give individuals freedom of religion. Articles 29–30 give communities rights to protect their culture and run educational institutions.
  • Personal laws for different religions reflect group recognition. The Uniform Civil Code debate (Article 44) is a liberal vs communitarian question.
  • In Shah Bano (1985), the Court upheld a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance. Parliament's 1986 Act was seen as yielding to community leaders. In Shayara Bano (2017), instant triple talaq was struck down.
  • Sabarimala (2018) pitted women's equality against a temple's customary ban on women aged 10 to 50.

Rajeev Bhargava calls Indian secularism "principled distance": the state engages with communities rather than staying fully neutral.

"Examine the communitarian critique of liberalism."
"Sandel's 'unencumbered self'. Comment."
"Explain Walzer's idea of complex equality."
"Is communitarianism a threat to individual rights?"

Structure: start with the liberal self (Rawls). Then give the four thinkers, one key idea each: Sandel's unencumbered self, MacIntyre's virtue and tradition, Taylor's atomism and recognition, Walzer's spheres. Then the liberal reply (Kymlicka, later Rawls) and the dangers. End with Indian examples: Articles 29–30, personal laws, Shah Bano, and Bhargava's principled distance.
